fields.label: Description
fields.value: The parts of the World Wide Web whose content is not indexed by standard web search-engine programs. Deep-web content may still be reachable through a direct URL, an authenticated session, a database query, a site-specific search interface, an archive, or specialized software.

value.source_scope_note: This record follows the supplied article text. Generalized structural links are represented as knowledge-graph relationships; they do not imply that every relationship was explicitly asserted in the article.

value.core_definition: Web content not indexed by standard search engines.

contrasted_with.surface_web: Content that is accessible and indexed by ordinary web search engines.
contrasted_with.dark_web: A subset of the deep web intentionally hidden and generally reachable through specialized software or networks rather than standard browsers and methods.

value.terminology_warning: Deep web and dark web are not synonyms. Media usage has sometimes conflated them, which has created persistent confusion.

historical_term_attribution.claim: Credited with establishing the term 'deep web' as a search-indexing term.

possible_access_requirements: Specialized software for certain intentionally hidden services

examples.name: Restricted social-media pages and profiles
examples.access_pattern: Privacy settings, account permissions, or login

examples.name: Paywalled video, magazine, and newspaper services
Web archives
examples.access_pattern: Archive interface and historical snapshot selection

value.name: Contextual web
value.description: Pages vary according to access context, such as client IP range or prior navigation sequence.
value.crawler_challenge: A crawler may not reproduce the context needed to obtain the same page.

value.name: Dynamic content
value.description: Pages are generated in response to submitted queries or forms and may not exist as stable, discoverable URLs before the query.
value.crawler_challenge: The query space may be too large or indeterminate to enumerate.

value.name: Limited-access content
value.description: Technical or policy controls limit crawling, indexing, or caching.
value.crawler_challenge: Access controls or directives can prevent crawling or cached copies.

value.name: Non-HTML or non-text content
value.description: Information is embedded in multimedia or file formats that a search engine may not recognize or extract.
value.crawler_challenge: Text extraction, format recognition, or semantic interpretation may be limited.

value.name: Private web
value.description: Resources require registration or login.
value.crawler_challenge: The crawler cannot retrieve the protected content without authorized access.

value.name: Scripted content
value.description: Pages or data are exposed through links created by JavaScript or content fetched dynamically by client-side scripts.
value.crawler_challenge: A crawler that does not execute the relevant scripts or reproduce application behavior may miss content.

value.name: Special-software-accessible content
value.description: Some intentionally hidden services are accessible through specialized software or networks.
value.crawler_challenge: Ordinary browsers and conventional crawlers do not directly access all such services.

value.name: Unlinked content
value.description: Pages with few or no links from known pages may remain undiscovered by link-following crawlers.
value.crawler_challenge: A crawler generally needs a known URL, link, sitemap, submission, or other discovery route.

value.name: Archived web content
value.description: Historical snapshots may be accessible through archival interfaces but may not be indexed as ordinary current pages.
value.classification_note: The supplied article describes archives as a possible deep-web case; classification can depend on the search engine and the particular archive resource.

value.name: Basic DHT put/get lifecycle

steps.action: Choose a logical object identifier such as a filename or content identifier.
Apply the system's hash/key derivation function to obtain key k.
Send put(k, data) to any participating DHT node.
Forward the message through the overlay toward the node responsible for k.
Store the key and value at the responsible node or configured replica set.
A reader derives the same key k and sends get(k) to any DHT node.
Route get(k) through the overlay and return the stored value or a result from a replica.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's 160-bit-key put/get walkthrough. Replication step is a general implementation option described elsewhere in the article.

value.name: Consistent-hashing membership change

steps.action: Assign each node an identifier in the abstract keyspace.
Assign each key to the closest node according to the algorithm's keyspace distance.
When a node joins or leaves, recompute affected ownership.
Transfer only keys whose responsible ownership changed, while other key assignments remain unchanged.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's description of consistent and rendezvous hashing.

value.name: Kademlia-style iterative lookup and publication

steps.action: Publish or discover node-presence information in the DHT.
Start a lookup for key k and consult known routing-table neighbors.
Query closer/suitable nodes iteratively instead of flooding every participant.
Select suitable nodes for storing or retrieving the value.
Send put(k, data) to those suitable nodes; use implementation-specific repair/self-healing when placement is stale.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's description of advanced DHTs such as Kademlia.

value.name: DHT Sybil threat and defense concepts

steps.action: An adversary attempts to participate under many identities.
Those identities may influence routing, key ownership, or availability depending on the DHT design.
Possible defenses discussed by the article include carefully designed Byzantine fault tolerance, Whanau-style design, and social-trust approaches.
Treat defenses as design-specific; the article describes the general Sybil-defense problem as an open research question.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's security section; this is an explanatory threat model, not a claim that every DHT is vulnerable in the same way.

overlay_families.description: Encapsulation/tunnel-based approaches that create logical connectivity over an underlay.
Provider and enterprise WAN overlays, including VPN and programmable SD-WAN approaches.
Overlays that organize peers or route using logical identifiers rather than only destination IP addresses.
Peer-based distribution over underlying unicast paths.
Systems named by the article among overlay networks; this grouping is a taxonomy aid and does not imply identical designs or guarantees.

value.benefit: Can identify and route to destinations independently of their currently known IP address.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires overlay-level naming, lookup, or routing mechanisms.

value.benefit: Can select overlay-node sequence and apply application/site/user-specific policies.
value.cost_or_limit: Cannot directly control the underlay's route between two overlay nodes.

value.benefit: Can detect path degradation and reroute at the overlay layer.
value.cost_or_limit: Still depends on lower-layer availability and may choose a longer path.

value.benefit: Can provide logical isolation and optionally encryption.
value.cost_or_limit: An overlay by itself does not guarantee confidentiality, authentication, or secure endpoint behavior.

value.benefit: Enables logical networks and tunnels over shared infrastructure.
value.cost_or_limit: Additional headers consume capacity and can affect MTU/fragmentation behavior (MTU note is model-expanded).

value.benefit: Can prioritize traffic by application, user, or site.
value.cost_or_limit: DiffServ prioritization does not itself guarantee end-to-end throughput.

value.benefit: Can distribute data among peers without relying on router-level IP multicast.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires maintaining an overlay topology and may create redundant transmissions.

value.name: Sign–Verify Lifecycle
value.description: Canonical public-key signature lifecycle from key generation through message signing and recipient verification.
controls: Validate signer-to-key binding
Reject if verification fails
Protect private key
Apply algorithm-specific encoding and parameters

value.name: PKI Identity Binding and Revocation
value.description: Establishes trust in the public key and checks current certificate status before relying on a signature.
controls: Do not infer key identity from signature alone
Check revocation status where required
Consider CA mis-issuance and PKI governance

value.name: Hash-Then-Sign
value.description: Hash the message, encode the digest according to the signature scheme, then sign the encoded digest.
controls: Never use raw RSA signing as described
Use suitable scheme-specific encoding
Hash the exact bytes whose semantics are intended to be signed

value.name: Hardware-Protected Signing Key
value.description: Keep signing key within a smart card or HSM and authorize signing requests through protected interfaces.
controls: Keep private key non-exportable where supported
Protect PIN entry against keylogging
Authenticate calling applications
Plan revocation after loss or theft

value.name: WYSIWYS Trusted Presentation
value.description: Ensures the user-facing semantic document corresponds to the exact bitstring presented to the signing operation.
controls: Prevent hidden content and semantic substitution
Ensure displayed and signed content match
Use integrity-checked applications

value.name: Replay-Safe Signed Transaction
value.description: Combines signature verification with application-level freshness and duplicate detection.
controls: Do not use signature bytes alone as transaction IDs
Bind transaction context, audience and freshness
Reject previously processed identifiers

value.name: Separate Signing and Encryption Keys
value.description: Uses distinct key pairs for legal assent/authentication and confidentiality so encrypted communication does not automatically imply a signed agreement.
controls: Never treat encryption as legal signature by itself
Use distinct lifecycle and recovery policies
Protect signing-key backups exceptionally carefully

value.rule: A signing private key must remain secret; anyone who obtains it can generate valid signatures.
Verify the signature against the exact received message bytes; any mutation should cause rejection under a correct scheme.
A valid signature proves control of a private key only relative to a trusted binding between that public key and the claimed identity.
A signature alone does not prevent replay; add transaction identifiers, freshness checks, and duplicate detection to state-changing protocols.
Do not assume signature bytes uniquely identify a signed message or transaction; account for randomized signatures and malleability.
Ensure the content the user sees and approves is the content actually signed; protect rendering and signing applications against substitution.
Check certificate/key status where the trust model requires it, especially after loss or suspected compromise.
Do not use raw/plain RSA as a signature construction; use a secure, scheme-appropriate hash-and-encoding construction.
Use separate key pairs for signing and encryption when the application needs to distinguish assent from confidentiality.
Hardware key storage reduces exposure but does not remove PIN, reader, application, provisioning, revocation, or user-interface risks.
Do not treat non-repudiation as an automatic mathematical or legal guarantee; key custody, identity binding, revocation timing, and jurisdiction matter.
Security requires a sound algorithm, correct implementation, correct protocol use, private-key secrecy, and trusted public-key ownership binding.
Do not assume signing hides a message or that encryption alone proves authenticity; combine mechanisms according to the required security goals.

value.name: Alice signs Hello Bob
value.scenario: Alice signs the bitstring Hello Bob with her private key; Bob receives message and signature and verifies with Alice's trusted public key.
flow: Bob validates Alice's public-key identity binding
Bob verifies signature and rejects if message was altered
value.lesson: Verification checks integrity and possession of the corresponding private key, assuming the public key is correctly associated with Alice.

value.name: Signed bank transfer and replay
value.scenario: A branch signs a transfer request. An attacker replays the same valid request if the bank lacks transaction IDs or duplicate detection.
flow: Attacker resends the same signed request
Without replay controls the transfer may execute again
Transaction ID and replay cache reject duplicate
value.lesson: Authentication and integrity do not provide freshness or exactly-once execution by themselves.

value.name: Authenticating a software update
value.scenario: Publisher distributes a non-secret patch; client verifies its signature before applying it to reduce risk of malicious substitution.
flow: Client verifies signature and trusted publisher key
value.lesson: A signature can authenticate public software artifacts even when confidentiality is unnecessary.

value.name: Smart-card digest signing
value.scenario: The application hashes a document and sends the digest to a smart card; the card signs using its stored private key and returns the signature.
flow: Signature is returned without exporting the private key
value.lesson: Hardware protection reduces key-extraction risk but does not by itself guarantee correct document presentation or safe host software.

value.name: Contract signing separate from encrypted negotiation
value.scenario: Parties exchange confidential negotiation messages using encryption keys and sign the final contract with separate signing keys.
flow: Each party signs the agreement with signing key
Signatures are verified against trusted identities
Compromise of one key type is handled according to its separate purpose
value.lesson: Encryption of a conversation should not be confused with signing a particular contract.

Compose and Swarm are the same.

value.core_problem: Package and execute applications consistently across differing computing environments while isolating processes, controlling resources, distributing images, coordinating multi-container applications, and supporting clustered container services.
value.central_model: Application + dependencies -> Dockerfile/build -> read-only image -> registry distribution -> container runtime -> isolated processes + shared kernel -> Compose/Swarm coordination -> persistent volumes where required.
value.central_insight: Docker is best understood as a connected packaging, runtime, distribution and orchestration ecosystem: images define reusable software artifacts, containers instantiate them, the Linux kernel supplies isolation/resource primitives, registries distribute artifacts, Compose coordinates applications, and Swarm clusters Docker Engines.

source_claims.claim: Docker packages software in lightweight containers using OS-level virtualization and automates deployment across environments.
Docker originated as a dotCloud internal project, debuted publicly in 2013, used LXC initially, then moved to libcontainer and later created Moby.
Docker adoption expanded through Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Oracle, Windows/WSL2, Docker Desktop licensing, AtomicJar, and major 2025 releases.
Docker uses Linux kernel interfaces, namespaces, cgroups and union-capable filesystems; macOS uses a Linux VM.
Docker software architecture includes dockerd, Docker CLI, Docker objects, registries and Dockerfiles.
Dockerfile example uses ARG, FROM, COPY, ENV, RUN, VOLUME and EXPOSE.
Docker Compose defines/runs multi-container applications and Docker Swarm provides clustering and Raft consensus.
Docker Volumes provide independent persistence and licensing differs between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop.
Related technologies include Linux, DevOps, gVisor, Kubernetes, microservices, OCI and related software architecture.

why_it_matters.core_problem: Package and execute applications consistently across differing computing environments while isolating processes, controlling resources, distributing images, coordinating multi-container applications, and supporting clustered container services.

value.name: Cryptographic hash function
value.definition: A deterministic algorithm that maps an arbitrary-length binary input to a fixed-length digest, with security goals including preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance.

value.primary_source: User-supplied Wikipedia article text: Cryptographic hash function
value.scope_note: The graph follows the supplied article's terminology and coverage, while adding explicit relationship structure, schema, patterns, and cautious engineering rules for machine use.
source_derived_content: Merkle–Damgård, wide-pipe, sponge, and HAIFA constructions
value.editorial_caveat: Algorithm status and parameter recommendations change. Use current standards and expert review for production decisions; the graph is not a substitute for a cryptographic design review.

value.name: Secure file verification
value.purpose: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.
steps: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.
caveats: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

value.name: Password storage with a password KDF
value.purpose: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.
steps: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.
caveats: Do not store plaintext passwords.
Do not use a fast hash such as raw SHA-256 or SHA-1 alone for password storage.
Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

value.name: HMAC message authentication
value.purpose: Authenticate messages using a shared secret and a standardized keyed construction.
steps: Agree on a secure hash and shared secret key.
Compute the HMAC over the canonical message representation.
Transmit the message and authentication tag.
Receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares tags using an appropriate constant-time comparison.
caveats: Do not substitute naive hash(secret || message) constructions for HMAC.
Key management and message canonicalization remain important.

value.name: Content-addressed storage
value.purpose: Address and deduplicate objects based on content.
steps: Select a collision-resistant hash and a canonical byte representation.
Hash the content to derive a content address.
Store the object and index its address to physical storage.
On retrieval, recompute the hash to verify content integrity.
caveats: Collision handling and algorithm migration should be part of the design.
The content address is not automatically a claim of publisher authenticity.

value.name: Merkle-tree verification
value.purpose: Commit to a large data set and verify components using a root digest and authentication path.
steps: Hash each leaf using an unambiguous encoding.
Hash internal nodes from their child hashes.
Publish or authenticate the root digest.
Verify a selected leaf by recomputing its path to the root.
caveats: Tree layout, leaf/node domain separation, and encoding must be specified to avoid ambiguity.

value.name: Hash-based proof of work
value.purpose: Make request creation moderately costly while allowing cheap validation.
steps: Define a target predicate over a hash output.
Vary a nonce or candidate header and compute hashes until the predicate passes.
Send the candidate and proof.
Verifier performs one or a small number of hash computations and checks the predicate.
caveats: Difficulty must be calibrated; proof of work does not itself establish the truth or legitimacy of the submitted content.

value.name: Cryptographic hash algorithm migration
value.purpose: Retire weak digest algorithms while maintaining interoperability.
steps: Inventory every algorithm use and stored identifier format.
Choose a modern algorithm appropriate to the use case and threat model.
Version formats and APIs so algorithm identity is explicit.
Where feasible, verify old objects and add new digests; plan dual-read or staged migration.
Monitor standards and cryptanalysis and retire obsolete formats.
caveats: A digest's byte length alone does not uniquely identify the algorithm.
Do not assume legacy digests become secure because they are combined with a modern digest.

value.statement: A cryptographic hash is not encryption and has no decryption key or general inverse operation.
A matching digest proves only a content match relative to the expected digest and trust chain; it does not establish that the content is safe or benign.
For an ideal n-bit hash, generic preimage work is about 2^n and generic collision work about 2^(n/2); real algorithms may be weaker due to cryptanalysis.
Fast general-purpose hashes should not be used alone to store passwords; use a salted password KDF with current recommended parameters.
For hash-based message authentication, use HMAC or another reviewed construction rather than naive secret-prefix/suffix hashing.
MD5 and SHA-1 are unsuitable for new applications that depend on collision resistance.
CRC-32 and similar checksums detect accidental corruption but do not provide cryptographic protection against intentional manipulation.
Persist the algorithm name/version and output parameters alongside a digest; digest bytes alone are not a robust self-describing identifier.

value.title: File digest comparison
value.input: A downloaded archive and a trusted SHA-256 digest string.
steps: Compute SHA-256 over the exact downloaded bytes.
Encode the result consistently, commonly as hexadecimal.
Compare with the authenticated expected digest.
value.output: Equal digests provide strong evidence of byte-for-byte identity under SHA-256's security assumptions and the trust model.

value.title: Leading-zero proof of work
value.input: A candidate message/header plus a nonce.
steps: Hash the candidate.
Check whether the digest begins with the required number of zero bits.
If not, vary the nonce and repeat.
value.output: A valid candidate is relatively cheap to verify; expected search effort grows exponentially with the number of required leading zero bits.

value.title: Digest commitment
value.input: A secret solution m held by Alice.
steps: Alice computes H(m) and publishes the digest before revealing m.
Bob later computes H(m) over the revealed solution.
They compare the result to the earlier commitment.
value.output: The matching digest supports the claim that the revealed solution matches the committed value, assuming the hash and protocol are appropriate.

value.title: Salted password verifier
value.input: Password candidate, unique random salt, KDF name and parameters.
steps: Derive a verifier with the selected password KDF.
Store the salt, algorithm parameters and verifier, not the plaintext password.
At login, derive again and compare.
value.output: Unique salts reduce cross-account precomputation and KDF cost slows each password guess.
